summary:
PyroSync is an interactive web application that helps users understand historical fire activity across Indonesia using NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations.

Although both satellite systems detect active fires, differences in spatial resolution, sensitivity, and observation timing make their raw hotspot counts difficult to compare across decades. PyroSync addresses this challenge through spatial standardization, temporal matching, and statistically evaluated cross-sensor calibration.

The platform brings together more than 10.9 million NASA FIRMS observations from five satellite platforms, spanning 2000–2026. Users can explore hotspot maps, select areas of interest, examine historical burning calendars, and identify unusual activity and critical burning periods.

PyroSync also provides transparent validation results, helping users distinguish original observations from experimental or validated harmonized estimates. By making long-term satellite fire records easier to interpret, PyroSync supports researchers, environmental organizations, and disaster-management teams in understanding recurring fire patterns and improving evidence-based preparedness.
details:
Project Details — PyroSync

What is PyroSync and how does it work?

PyroSync is an interactive web application designed to make more than two decades of satellite fire observations easier to understand, compare, and use. Our project addresses NASA's challenge of harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data into a historical burning activity calendar.

NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments have monitored active fires for years, but their observations are not directly comparable. MODIS has an approximately 1 km active-fire pixel resolution, while VIIRS provides 375 m observations. This means a single fire can produce different numbers of detected hotspots depending on the satellite observing it.

PyroSync addresses this problem by combining five satellite platforms: MODIS Terra, MODIS Aqua, VIIRS Suomi NPP, VIIRS NOAA-20, and VIIRS NOAA-21.

Our application processes these observations through several stages:

  1. Spatial and temporal harmonization: Organizing observations into consistent geographical grids and aligning detections by date and acquisition time.
  2. Statistical calibration: Converting eligible satellite observations into a common MODIS Aqua-equivalent measurement scale using historical periods when the instruments overlap.
  3. Multi-sensor fusion: Combining calibrated observations using an availability-aware average rather than simply adding raw hotspot counts, which could count the same fire multiple times.
  4. Historical analysis: Transforming the resulting data into interactive maps, burning calendars, seasonal trends, and indicators of unusual or sustained elevated activity.

The application currently contains 10,917,537 NASA FIRMS observations across Indonesia, spanning November 2000 to November 2026.

What can users do with PyroSync?

We wanted PyroSync to be useful even for people without programming or remote-sensing experience.

Users can explore Indonesia through an interactive map, choose administrative regions, draw custom areas, or click a location to examine nearby fire activity. The map automatically adjusts its grid resolution as users zoom in or out.

The platform also provides several connected features:

  • Interactive Fire Map: Explore satellite-detected hotspots and harmonized activity through geographic visualizations.
  • Burning Activity Calendar: Identify when fire activity was higher or lower during particular months and years.
  • Historical Patterns: Compare seasonal and long-term observations to understand recurring burning periods.
  • AOI Insights: Examine unusual activity, recurring hotspots, and historically critical periods.
  • Harmonization Diagnostics: Inspect sensor differences, calibration results, validation checks, and the scientific limitations of the analysis.
  • Data Export: Download available observations and analytical results for further investigation.

What makes PyroSync innovative?

The innovation is not simply displaying satellite hotspots, because NASA FIRMS already provides that information.

Our main innovation is connecting satellite observations from different generations into a more comparable historical record and making that record accessible through one interactive application.

Rather than treating every satellite detection as equivalent, PyroSync accounts for differences in sensor characteristics and availability. Our harmonization approach also preserves the original measurements so users can examine how the results were produced.

We tested the fusion method against MODIS Aqua observations using chronological holdout evaluation. For Indonesia-wide daily totals, the model achieved a mean absolute error of 35.7 detections per day, compared with 515.8 for the uncalibrated multi-sensor average. The model passed our project's national-level validation criteria, although regional and individual grid-cell results still have important limitations.

This transparency is part of our approach: we want users to understand not only what the satellite data show, but also how reliable a particular comparison is.

Who benefits from this project?

PyroSync is intended for environmental researchers, disaster-management organizations, forestry agencies, conservation groups, and communities interested in understanding historical fire activity.

For example, disaster-management teams can examine which months have repeatedly experienced high fire activity when preparing seasonal monitoring strategies. Forestry and conservation organizations can identify areas with recurring satellite detections and prioritize further investigation. Researchers can compare historical periods without manually processing millions of records from different satellite instruments.

By putting this information into an accessible web application, PyroSync can reduce the technical effort required to explore long-term fire patterns and support more informed environmental planning.

However, PyroSync is not a replacement for official emergency alerts, ground verification, or wildfire forecasting systems. Its observations represent satellite-detected thermal activity, not independently confirmed forest-fire incidents.

Technology and development tools

PyroSync was developed using:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, and Apache ECharts.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Data processing: DuckDB, numerical and statistical methods, and custom harmonization algorithms.
  • Satellite data: NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire products.
  • Satellite imagery: NASA Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS), where available.
  • Development and deployment: Git, GitHub, and Vercel.

Our team prioritized scientific transparency, historical data availability, map usability, performance, and accessibility.

We also considered the limitations of satellite observations, including clouds, different overpass times, changing sensor availability, and differences in detection sensitivity.

Intended impact

Our goal is to transform a complex collection of satellite observations into a practical historical fire-information tool.

By combining multi-sensor harmonization with interactive geographic exploration, PyroSync helps users move beyond simply asking "Where are hotspots being detected?" toward more useful questions:

"How has observed fire activity changed over time, which areas repeatedly experience high activity, and how much can we trust comparisons between different satellite generations?"

We believe answering these questions more clearly can help communities, researchers, and decision-makers better understand historical fire patterns and prepare for future fire seasons.
